title: Suspected Measles
bottomLine: Suspected measles is an airborne/public-health problem before the lab confirms it. Mask the client if tolerated, isolate from shared air/traffic, use fit-tested respiratory protection, and notify infection prevention/public health promptly.
recognize: Maculopapular rash beginning on face and spreading downward
differentiate: Other viral exanthems lack the classic respiratory prodrome/Koplik pattern
Drug eruptions do not remove the need to isolate a compatible outbreak case until assessed
medicationSafety: Post-exposure MMR versus immune globulin depends on age, immune status, pregnancy and timing
Do not independently choose PEP outside public-health guidance
followUp: Public-health directed follow-up and exposure monitoring
examTrap: Waiting for lab confirmation before airborne precautions or placing the client in a common waiting room.
oneLinePearl: Measles: isolate the air first, confirm the diagnosis second.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada measles guidance

title: Pertussis
bottomLine: Pertussis is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can be catastrophic in young infants. Recognize prolonged/paroxysmal cough, protect vulnerable contacts, use droplet/source-control measures, and coordinate treatment/contact management with current public-health guidance.
recognize: Apnea/cyanosis can be the infant presentation
differentiate: Viral cough usually lacks prolonged paroxysmal pattern
Asthma causes episodic airflow obstruction rather than the classic pertussis exposure/cough course
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice/dose depends on age, pregnancy, interactions and local guidance
Early treatment reduces transmission more than it reverses late cough
examTrap: Assuming absence of a 'whoop' excludes pertussis, especially in infants.
oneLinePearl: Pertussis in an infant may be apnea—not a dramatic whoop.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada pertussis guidance

title: Rabies Exposure and Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
bottomLine: Rabies is almost universally fatal after symptoms begin, so exposure assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis are time-sensitive. Clean the wound immediately and involve public health for animal-risk assessment and vaccine/immune-globulin planning.
recognize: Bite/scratch or mucous-membrane exposure to potentially rabid mammal
Bat exposure can require careful history
Risk depends on animal, geography and availability for testing/observation
differentiate: Not every animal contact is a rabies exposure
Tetanus and bacterial wound risk are separate issues that must also be assessed
management: Rabies immune globulin for eligible previously unvaccinated exposures
medicationSafety: PEP schedule differs by previous vaccination and immune status
Do not inject immune globulin into the same site as vaccine
counselling: Complete the entire prescribed PEP series
Do not delay while trying to capture an animal unsafely
examTrap: Waiting for symptoms before acting or treating rabies PEP as optional after a high-risk exposure.
oneLinePearl: Rabies prevention works before symptoms—wash, assess, and start PEP when indicated.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada rabies guidance

title: Meningococcal Close-Contact Management
bottomLine: Invasive meningococcal disease demands rapid treatment of the case and prompt identification of true close contacts for chemoprophylaxis/public-health follow-up. Casual contact is not automatically a prophylaxis indication.
recognize: Direct exposure to oral/nasal secretions can matter
differentiate: Casual workplace/classroom proximity is different from high-risk secretion exposure
Vaccination status does not automatically eliminate all contact-management decisions
management: Vaccination when public health recommends it
medicationSafety: Prophylactic drug selection depends on age, pregnancy, contraindications and local guidance
counselling: Seek emergency care immediately for compatible symptoms
Explain why some contacts receive prophylaxis and others do not
examTrap: Giving prophylaxis to every casual contact while missing the symptomatic contact who needs emergency assessment.
oneLinePearl: Meningococcus: treat disease now; public health defines who needs prophylaxis.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada invasive meningococcal disease guidance

title: Mpox Community Care
bottomLine: Mpox commonly causes painful lesions with systemic symptoms. Use appropriate infection-control precautions, assess pain/hydration and high-risk status, provide non-stigmatizing sexual-health/public-health teaching, and escalate ocular, airway, neurologic, pregnancy, immunocompromised, or extensive disease.
differentiate: Varicella, HSV, syphilis and bacterial skin disease can mimic lesions
Exposure history supports but does not replace diagnostic testing
management: Public-health notification and antiviral/specialist assessment for severe/high-risk cases
medicationSafety: Antiviral access/indication follows public-health/specialist pathways
Avoid stigmatizing assumptions about exposure
counselling: Cover lesions and follow current public-health exposure/isolation guidance
followUp: Public-health follow-up until recovery criteria met
examTrap: Treating mpox as only a sexual-orientation diagnosis or ignoring severe pain/ocular disease.
oneLinePearl: Mpox care = protect contacts, control pain, check eyes/airway/immunity, avoid stigma.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada mpox guidance

title: Kawasaki Disease
bottomLine: Persistent fever plus evolving mucocutaneous inflammation in a young child can be Kawasaki disease; infants may have incomplete presentations. Early IVIG-based treatment reduces coronary complications, so track fever duration and do not wait for every classic feature.
differentiate: Scarlet fever/toxic shock/viral illnesses can mimic parts of the syndrome
Incomplete Kawasaki is especially important in infants
workup: Inflammatory labs and CBC as ordered
medicationSafety: Monitor IVIG infusion reactions
Live-vaccine timing may change after IVIG
Antiplatelet therapy requires bleeding/Rx teaching
examTrap: Excluding Kawasaki in an infant because not all classic features are present.
oneLinePearl: Five days of fever plus mucocutaneous clues: think Kawasaki before the coronaries pay the price.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society Kawasaki disease guidance

title: Orbital Cellulitis
bottomLine: Pain with eye movement, restricted extraocular movement, proptosis, reduced vision, or systemic illness suggests orbital—not simple preseptal—cellulitis. Protect vision and prevent intracranial spread with urgent imaging/specialty assessment and IV antibiotics.
differentiate: Preseptal cellulitis has eyelid inflammation without orbital signs such as painful/restricted EOM or proptosis
Allergic swelling is usually bilateral/itchy without fever/orbital dysfunction
workup: Urgent imaging when orbital disease suspected
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice follows local pediatric/infection guidance
Do not delay therapy for nonessential testing in a deteriorating child
counselling: Return urgently for visual change/worsening swelling
examTrap: Calling every swollen eyelid preseptal cellulitis without checking vision and eye movements.
oneLinePearl: Eye movement pain + proptosis/vision change = orbit emergency.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric infectious-disease guidance

title: Pediatric Acute Kidney Injury
bottomLine: Pediatric AKI can present as falling urine output, edema, hypertension, electrolyte change, or rising creatinine. Accurate weight-based fluid balance and medication/nephrotoxin review are nursing priorities; hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe oliguria, or neurologic change require urgent escalation.
differentiate: Dehydration may be prerenal and reversible; obstruction/intrinsic renal injury need different source treatment
Normal creatinine does not always reassure early in a small child without trend/context
medicationSafety: Many drugs require renal dose review
NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion in dehydrated children
examTrap: Giving repeated fluid boluses to an edematous/overloaded child simply because urine output is low.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric AKI: weigh, measure every mL, check potassium, know whether the child is dry or overloaded.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric kidney-care guidance

title: Pediatric Acute Migraine
bottomLine: Most recurrent pediatric migraine is benign, but the nursing job is to screen for secondary-headache red flags before treating pain. Use weight-appropriate therapy early, reduce triggers, and escalate abnormal neurologic findings, thunderclap onset, meningismus, trauma, or progressive pattern change.
differentiate: Meningitis adds fever/neck stiffness/systemic illness
Raised ICP may cause progressive morning headache/vomiting/neurologic signs
Thunderclap headache requires emergency evaluation
workup: No routine imaging for a typical stable migraine without red flags
Urgent imaging/labs when secondary cause suspected
medicationSafety: Avoid medication overuse
Doses are weight/age dependent
followUp: Primary care/neurology follow-up for frequent or disabling migraine
examTrap: Ordering emergency imaging for every typical recurrent migraine—or, opposite, dismissing a new focal deficit as migraine.
oneLinePearl: Treat the migraine, but first prove the headache has no red flags.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric migraine guidance

title: Pediatric Skin and Soft-Tissue Infection
bottomLine: Cellulitis is diffuse skin infection; a fluctuant collection is an abscess that may need drainage. Rapid pain/progression, toxicity, crepitus, orbital/perineal location, or immunocompromise are red flags for deeper or invasive infection.
recognize: Fever may or may not occur
differentiate: Contact dermatitis is usually itchy and exposure-patterned
Necrotizing infection causes pain/toxicity out of proportion
Insect-bite inflammation is not automatically bacterial
medicationSafety: Antibiotic selection reflects age, allergy, local resistance and purulent/nonpurulent pattern
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics for noninfectious inflammation
counselling: Return for fever, progression, or poor response
examTrap: Treating a fluctuant abscess with oral antibiotics alone while ignoring source control.
oneLinePearl: Cellulitis needs antimicrobial assessment; abscess needs source control.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric skin/soft-tissue infection guidance

title: Buprenorphine-Naloxone Induction
bottomLine: Buprenorphine's high opioid-receptor affinity can relieve withdrawal—or precipitate it if standard induction begins before sufficient withdrawal from a full agonist. Follow the prescribed induction strategy, assess objective withdrawal/exposure, and monitor sedation and breathing.
recognize: Precipitated withdrawal: abrupt severe worsening soon after first dose
differentiate: Untreated withdrawal builds according to opioid pharmacology; precipitated withdrawal worsens abruptly after buprenorphine
Overdose causes sedation/bradypnea rather than adrenergic withdrawal
management: Treat precipitated withdrawal per clinician plan
medicationSafety: Alcohol/benzodiazepines increase sedation/overdose risk
Do not start a standard induction solely because a clock interval passed
counselling: OAT is maintenance treatment, not a moral failure or quick detox
examTrap: Giving buprenorphine too early because 'enough hours' passed without assessing the actual opioid and withdrawal state.
oneLinePearl: Buprenorphine induction follows withdrawal physiology—not the clock alone.

title: Methadone OAT Safety
bottomLine: Methadone is effective OAT but accumulates and can cause delayed respiratory depression, especially during induction or with other sedatives. Verify the dose, assess sedation/respiration, avoid duplicate dosing, and recognize QT/interactions and lost-tolerance risk.
recognize: Sedation or slow breathing after dose
Risk rises early in titration and with alcohol/benzodiazepines
differentiate: Withdrawal causes autonomic activation; toxicity causes sedation/respiratory depression
medicationSafety: Long/variable half-life means toxicity can be delayed
QT prolongation and drug interactions matter
Tolerance falls after interruption
followUp: Reassess after missed doses or medication changes
examTrap: Administering a methadone dose from memory when the dose or recent adherence cannot be verified.
oneLinePearl: Methadone safety = verify dose, check breathing, respect accumulation and lost tolerance.

title: Benzodiazepine Withdrawal
bottomLine: Abrupt benzodiazepine cessation after physiologic dependence can cause severe anxiety, tremor, autonomic symptoms, delirium, and seizures. Do not advise abrupt discontinuation; high-risk withdrawal needs monitored, clinician-directed taper/treatment.
recognize: Risk relates to dose, duration, agent half-life and abrupt cessation
differentiate: Alcohol withdrawal has a similar syndrome and may coexist
Panic disorder does not cause withdrawal seizures simply from missed medication
assessment: Drug, dose, duration and last use
workup: Electrolytes/other tests for severe illness as ordered
medicationSafety: Abrupt stopping can be dangerous
Concurrent opioids increase overdose risk while taking benzodiazepines
counselling: Do not stop long-term benzodiazepines suddenly
Use one coordinated prescriber/pharmacy plan when possible
followUp: Treat underlying anxiety/sleep disorder with safer long-term strategies
examTrap: Telling a dependent client to 'just stop' benzodiazepines immediately.
oneLinePearl: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can seize—taper, assess, monitor.

title: Stimulant Intoxication
bottomLine: Cocaine/methamphetamine intoxication can produce agitation, hyperthermia, severe hypertension, chest pain, dysrhythmia, seizure, or psychosis. Reduce stimulation, protect staff/client safety, monitor temperature/cardiovascular status, and escalate medical instability immediately.
differentiate: Serotonin syndrome/NMS have medication-context and neuromuscular patterns
Panic alone should not explain severe hyperthermia, ischemic chest pain, or seizure
workup: Glucose/electrolytes/CK/troponin or other testing as clinically indicated
medicationSafety: Avoid escalating agitation through confrontational care
Specific cardiovascular drug choices require clinician direction
counselling: Harm reduction and non-stigmatizing substance-use support
examTrap: Treating severe agitation as only a behavioural problem and missing hyperthermia or cardiac toxicity.
oneLinePearl: Stimulant agitation is medical until temperature, heart, brain, and glucose are safe.

title: Opioid Withdrawal and OAT Engagement
bottomLine: Opioid withdrawal is miserable and destabilizing but usually not directly fatal in a healthy adult; the larger danger is relapse and overdose after tolerance falls. Treat symptoms, offer evidence-based OAT, provide naloxone, and avoid punitive care.
differentiate: Opioid overdose causes sedation and respiratory depression—the opposite physiology
Alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal carries greater seizure/delirium risk
workup: Testing guided by comorbidity/complication rather than punishment
medicationSafety: Lost tolerance raises overdose risk after abstinence
OAT dosing follows an authorized plan
counselling: OAT reduces morbidity/mortality and should be offered without stigma
Carry naloxone and avoid using alone
examTrap: Treating withdrawal as a reason to deny care or sending the client away without OAT/naloxone linkage.
oneLinePearl: Withdrawal hurts; lost tolerance kills—engage OAT and overdose prevention.
